games.name: Set
games.kit: A Set card deck (81 cards) costs about 13 dollars. Printing and cutting cards with shape, colour, number and shading at home costs nothing.
games.teaches: Every player scans for combinations that are all the same or all different across four attributes at once. It is fast pattern matching under a ticking clock.
games.rules:
1. Lay out 12 cards face up in a grid.
2. Every card has four attributes: shape, colour, number and shading.
3. Call "Set" when three cards make each attribute all the same or all different across the three.
4. Take your three cards, then deal three more from the deck to refill the grid.
5. If nobody sees a set, deal three extra cards without removing any.
6. When the deck runs out, the player with the most sets wins.

First strategy: scan one attribute at a time across the whole grid instead of guessing whole cards.

Variation: play five minute speed rounds and compare scores across rounds instead of playing out the whole deck.
games.notice: Watch for a called set where one attribute is two the same and one different. That near miss is the exact mistake this game trains the eye to catch.

games.name: Mastermind
games.kit: A Mastermind set with pegs and a code board, about 12 dollars.
games.teaches: Every guess is a question and the peg feedback is the answer. The codebreaker combines several answers in a row to narrow down one true code.
games.rules:
1. One player sets a secret code of four coloured pegs behind the screen.
2. The other player guesses four pegs in a row.
3. Black pegs mean right colour, right spot. White pegs mean right colour, wrong spot.
4. The guesser uses that feedback to make a better guess next turn.
5. The game ends when the guesser matches the code exactly or runs out of rows.
6. Swap roles and compare how many guesses each of you needed.

First strategy: after your first guess, change only what the feedback says is wrong and keep everything it confirms.

Variation: play with five colours instead of six to shorten the game for a first try.
games.notice: Watch for a guess that ignores feedback from an earlier turn, information from every past guess still counts.

games.name: Dots and boxes
games.kit: A printed grid of dots, free, and two pens in different colours.
games.teaches: Every line drawn either does nothing, gives away a box, or starts a chain. Counting the chains left decides who is forced to open the next one.
games.rules:
1. Draw a grid of dots.
2. Take turns drawing one line between two neighbouring dots.
3. If your line completes the fourth side of a box, write your initial in it and go again.
4. If your line does not complete a box, play passes to the other player.
5. When all lines are drawn, count the boxes; the most boxes wins.
6. Near the end, watch for chains of boxes joined in a row.

First strategy: when you must open a chain, open the shortest one so your opponent gets the fewest free boxes from it.

Variation: play a 3 by 3 grid of boxes for a five minute game, or 5 by 5 for a longer one.
games.notice: Watch for a player who takes every free box without noticing they are opening a long chain for the other side next.

games.name: Hex
games.kit: A printed Hex board, free, with two colours of counters or beads, or a boxed Hex set for about 20 dollars.
games.teaches: Each player owns two opposite sides of a hex grid. One player always manages to connect their two sides, and a draw is mathematically impossible.
games.rules:
1. Each player owns two opposite sides of the diamond shaped board.
2. Take turns placing one stone of your colour on any empty hexagon.
3. After the very first stone is placed, the other player may swap sides instead of moving, taking over that stone and cancelling its advantage.
4. Build an unbroken chain of your stones from one of your sides to the other.
5. Blocking your opponent's chain and building your own often happen with the same move.
6. The first player to complete a connected chain wins.
7. If the board fills up, one side has always connected; check the corners first.

First strategy: play near the centre first, since central hexagons touch more of the board than edge ones.

Variation: play on a smaller 7 by 7 board for a faster first game.
games.notice: Watch for a family argument over whether a draw is possible. Play the board all the way full, and it always finishes with a winner.

games.name: Guess my rule
games.kit: A deck of playing cards, free if already in the house.
games.teaches: One player invents a secret rule for which cards can follow which. Everyone else proposes cards and learns from true or false, exactly like testing a hypothesis.
games.rules:
1. One player, the rule maker, secretly writes down a rule for which cards can follow which.
2. The rule maker lays down one card to start the row.
3. Each other player in turn plays a card they guess fits the rule.
4. The rule maker says whether it fits; a wrong card is set aside face up as a clue instead of removed from play.
5. Players use the fitting and non-fitting cards to guess the rule out loud.
6. Whoever guesses the exact rule first becomes the next rule maker.

First strategy: after a wrong guess, ask what changed between the last two cards instead of guessing a whole new rule from scratch.

Variation: write the rule down at the start. Reveal it after three correct guesses in a row, so everyone can check their thinking against it.
games.notice: Watch for a player who keeps guessing without tracking what every past card has already told them, the game rewards keeping notes.

games.name: The 24 game
games.kit: A 24 Game card deck, about 15 dollars, or a regular deck of playing cards with face cards removed, free.
games.teaches: Four numbers combine with add, subtract, multiply and divide in many different orders. Only some orders reach exactly 24, and order of operations decides which.
games.rules:
1. Deal one card showing four numbers, or draw four cards from a regular deck.
2. Every player works at once to make the four numbers equal exactly 24.
3. You may add, subtract, multiply or divide, and use each number exactly once.
4. The first player to say a working combination out loud wins the card.
5. Check the arithmetic together before awarding the card.
6. Whoever holds the most cards after an agreed number of rounds wins.

First strategy: look for two numbers that combine into a useful middle number like 6, 8 or 12 before worrying about the other two.

Variation: allow exponents for older players, or require a full written equation before calling out the answer.
games.notice: Watch for an answer that reaches 24 by using one number twice or skipping another, check that every number was used exactly once.

games.name: Kerbal Space Program
games.kit: Kerbal Space Program on a Windows, Mac or Linux PC, about 40 dollars, and a PC able to run it.
games.teaches: An orbit is a fall that keeps missing the ground because it moves sideways fast enough. Delta-v is the fuel budget that pays for every change of speed and direction.
games.rules:
1. Build a simple rocket with the in-game parts and a command pod.
2. Launch straight up, then tip the rocket sideways as speed builds, so it starts falling around the planet instead of onto it.
3. Watch the orbit line: a closed oval around the planet means you are officially in orbit, endlessly falling and missing.
4. Check the delta-v readout before every burn; it is the fuel budget for everything you still want to do.
5. Plan one manoeuvre, such as raising the far side of the orbit, and burn only as much delta-v as that manoeuvre needs.
6. Return safely, then look at how much delta-v is left for the next mission.

First strategy: build a rocket with more delta-v than the mission needs, since a mission rarely fails from carrying too much fuel.

Variation: take turns as pilot and mission control, where mission control reads out the delta-v budget before every burn.
games.notice: Watch for a launch straight up with no sideways tip, that reaches space but falls straight back down instead of reaching orbit.

games.name: Battleship
games.kit: A Battleship set, about 15 dollars, or two printed grids and pencils, free.
games.teaches: Calling out coordinates finds a hidden ship fastest when each guess splits the remaining board roughly in half instead of guessing at random.
games.rules:
1. Each player secretly places ships of different lengths on a grid, hidden behind a screen.
2. Take turns calling out one coordinate, such as D5.
3. The other player says hit or miss, and must announce when a ship is sunk.
4. Mark every call on a second grid so you remember what you have already tried.
5. The first player to sink every one of the other's ships wins.
6. Compare how many calls each of you needed to win.

First strategy: once you score a hit, check the four neighbouring coordinates next instead of jumping somewhere new.

Variation: agree on a smaller 6 by 6 grid with shorter ships for a faster game.
games.notice: Watch for a call that repeats a coordinate already tried, the marked grid exists so that never has to happen.

games.name: Rubik's cube
games.teaches: A solving algorithm is a fixed sequence of moves that can be undone. A commutator is a short sequence and its opposite, and it swaps a few pieces while leaving the rest alone.
games.rules:
1. One player scrambles the cube with about twenty random turns while the other looks away.
2. The solver works through the layers in order: one face, then the middle layer, then the last layer.
3. Say each algorithm out loud as a sequence of moves, such as turn right, turn top, turn right back.
4. If a sequence does not do what you expected, turn it in reverse to undo it exactly.
5. Time how long the solve takes.
6. Swap jobs and compare times.

First strategy: finish one layer completely before touching the next; do not try to fix the whole cube in one move.

Variation: learn one commutator, a sequence that swaps two pieces and leaves the rest alone, then use it on the last layer.
games.notice: Watch for a random search of turns with no plan, a memorised sequence beats guessing every single time.

games.name: Sprouts
games.teaches: Every dot can take at most three lines. Euler's formula for a flat drawing quietly limits how many moves the whole game can possibly last.
games.rules:
1. Draw two or three dots on paper to start.
2. On your turn, draw one line connecting two dots, or a dot to itself, without crossing any other line.
3. Add a new dot somewhere in the middle of the line you just drew.
4. No dot may ever have more than three lines touching it.
5. If a player cannot draw a legal line, that player loses.
6. Play again and try to last one more move than last time.

First strategy: avoid boxing a dot in early, since a dot with three lines already is dead for the rest of the game.

Variation: start with four dots instead of two or three for a longer game.
games.notice: Watch for a running count of how many dots are already full, that count predicts roughly how many moves are left in the game.

games.name: Blokus
games.teaches: Every new piece must touch your own colour only at a corner, never along a flat edge. Packing shapes under that one rule decides who runs out of room first.
games.rules:
1. Each player takes all 21 pieces in one colour.
2. Place your first piece touching your own corner of the board.
3. Every later piece must touch your own colour, but only at a corner. It may not touch your own colour along a flat edge.
4. Pieces may touch or cover other players' pieces along any edge.
5. If you cannot legally place a piece, pass for the rest of the game.
6. When nobody can move, count squares placed; the most squares wins.

First strategy: place your biggest, most awkward pieces early, while the board still has room for their shape.

Variation: play a shorter game on a smaller board taped off from a full Blokus board.
games.notice: Watch for a piece placed touching your own colour along a flat edge, that placement is not legal and must be redone.

games.name: Quarto
games.teaches: Every piece is tall or short, light or dark, round or square, and hollow or solid. The twist is that your opponent chooses which piece you must place next.
games.rules:
1. Lay out all 16 pieces where both players can see every attribute.
2. Choose a piece and hand it to the other player.
3. The other player places that piece anywhere on the 4 by 4 board.
4. That player then chooses a piece and hands it back to you.
5. If four pieces in a row, column or diagonal share any one attribute, whoever placed the last piece wins.
6. If the board fills with no line of four, the game is a draw.

First strategy: before handing over a piece, check whether it completes a line for your opponent no matter where they place it.

Variation: also count the four corners and the four centre squares as winning lines for a harder game.
games.notice: Watch for a piece handed over that wins no matter where it lands. That is the single mistake this game trains a player to stop making.
